Black-Box Skill Stealing Attack from Proprietary LLM Agents: An Empirical Study

Zihan Wang    Rui Zhang    Yu Liu    Chi Liu    Qingchuan Zhao    Hongwei Li    Guowen Xu ††thanks: Corresponding author: Guowen Xu (email: guowen.xu@uestc.edu.cn).
Abstract

LLM agents increasingly rely on skills to encapsulate reusable capabilities via progressively disclosed instructions. High-quality skills inject expert knowledge into general-purpose models, improving performance on specialized tasks. This quality and ease of dissemination drive the emergence of a skill economy: free skill marketplaces already report 90368 published skills, while paid marketplaces report more than 2000 listings and over $100,000 in creator earnings. Yet this growing marketplace also creates a new attack surface, as adversaries can interact with public agent to extract hidden proprietary skill content. We present the first empirical study of black-box skill stealing against LLM agent systems. To study this threat, we first derive an attack taxonomy from prior prompt-stealing methods and build an automated stealing prompt generation agent. This agent starts from model-generated seed prompts, expands them through scenario rationalization and structure injection, and enforces diversity via embedding filtering. This process yields a reproducible pipeline for evaluating agent systems. We evaluate such attacks across 3 commercial agent architectures and 5 LLMs. Our results show that agent skills can be extracted with only 3 interactions, posing a serious copyright risk. To mitigate this threat, we design defenses across three stages of the agent pipeline: input, inference, and output. Although these defenses achieve strong results, the attack remains inexpensive and readily automatable, allowing an adversary to launch repeated attempts with different variants; only one successful attempt is sufficient to compromise the protected skill. Overall, our findings suggest that these copyright risks are largely overlooked across proprietary agent ecosystems. We therefore advocate for more robust defense strategies that provide stronger protection guarantees.

I Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being deployed in coding assistants, productivity tools, and domain-specific automation systems [2, 3, 4, 5]. As these systems mature, developers are relying more heavily on modular abstractions to organize and scale agent behavior. Among these abstractions, skills have emerged as a practical mechanism for packaging reusable capabilities, including task instructions, workflow constraints, tool-use logic, supporting resources, and domain knowledge [6, 7, 8]. High-quality skills can further inject domain-expert knowledge, curated workflows, and execution constraints into otherwise general-purpose models, making them especially valuable in specialized application settings. This value and ease of dissemination has already produced an emerging skill economy: a public dashboard built from skills.sh data reports 90,368 published skills, 9,485 publishers, and 24.3M cumulative installs as of March 31, 2026 [9]. In parallel, paid marketplaces have started to sell validated skills as reusable digital products. As illustrated in Fig. 1, Claw Mart presents itself as “the app store for AI assistants,” reports 2,000+ listings and $100,000+ earned by creators, and explicitly markets paid skills and personas as downloadable digital goods [1, 10]. More broadly, this trend enables creators to package expert knowledge and carefully engineered workflows into portable skills that can be distributed or monetized through public marketplaces.

The rapid growth and commercial potential of these marketplaces introduce a new attack surface. Once a valuable skill is stored as a hidden yet repeatedly loaded artifact, unauthorized extraction is no longer merely prompt leakage; it constitutes theft of a transferable capability. Such a capability often extends beyond prompt text to include curated workflows, templates, scripts, and domain-specific operational knowledge [6, 7, 8]. Unauthorized extraction therefore poses a serious copyright and economic threat: once leaked, a proprietary skill can be copied, redistributed, and even resold at almost no cost, seriously violating the creator’s rights.

In this paper, we first study skill stealing, a black-box extraction attack in which an adversary interacts with a public agent interface and attempts to recover hidden proprietary skill content through carefully crafted prompts. Compared with system prompts, skills are more modular, more structured, and more directly tied to marketplace distribution and monetization [6, 7, 8]. These properties make leakage more actionable for attackers and more damaging for skill providers. The central questions are therefore whether existing prompt-stealing techniques can be transferred effectively to the skill setting, and how effective defenses can be designed to protect against skill extraction.

To answer this question, we derive a attack taxonomy from prior prompt-stealing work and use it to build an automated skill stealing prompt generation agent framework. Our framework starts from model-generated seed prompts and systematically instantiates them with scenario rationalization and structure injection strategies, while enforcing diversity through embedding-based filtering. This process yields a benchmark that operationalizes skill stealing as a reproducible black-box evaluation problem over commercial agent systems and closed-source models.

Using this benchmark, we evaluate skill stealing across three commercial agent architectures, five representative LLMs, and four complementary leakage metrics. The results show that black-box extraction of proprietary skills is not only practical in realistic deployments, but also easy to carry out and effective across a wide range of settings. We further evaluate prompt-level defenses adapted from prior prompt-stealing literature and find that their protection is limited against diverse automated extraction. We therefore design lightweight defenses centered on input detection, inference hardening, and output filtering, which achieve excellent results in mitigating these attacks. Although these defenses achieve strong results on parts of the benchmark, such improvements are still not enough to remove the broader concern. With our attack, an adversary can cheaply and automatically launch many repeated attempts using different variants, and only a single successful extraction is enough to cause serious copyright harm.

Overall, our findings suggest that the copyright risks surrounding skills are largely overlooked across proprietary agent ecosystems. We therefore advocate for more robust defense strategies that provide stronger protection guarantees. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We first identify and formulate skill stealing as a new security threat against agent systems, where proprietary skills can be illicitly extracted through adversarial prompting.

  • •

    We develop an automated agent framework for generating diverse and effective skill-stealing prompts, grounded in our proposed taxonomy of prompt-stealing attacks.

  • •

    We build a benchmark with 12 types of skill stealing attacks using the proposed framework and use it to evaluate representative closed-source models and commercial agent platforms. Our study provides a detailed analysis of attack effectiveness, leakage patterns, and the limitations of existing defenses.

  • •

    We further design three lightweight defenses targeting the input, context, and output stages of agent systems. Although these defenses reduce leakage risks in practice, our results suggest that they are insufficient to fully prevent skill stealing, calling for stronger protection mechanisms in future agent ecosystems.

II Related Work and Preliminary

II-A LLM agent skills

LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable capability modules, rather than repeatedly encoding task procedures in monolithic prompts. Skills serve precisely this role. In agent systems, a skill packages how a recurring class of tasks should be solved, bridging general-purpose model capabilities with task-specific operational behavior [6, 7, 8]. The growing importance of skills is also evident in today’s agent ecosystem, where major model providers have begun to expose skill-like capability packaging as an explicit agent abstraction [6, 7]. Together, these developments suggest that skills are becoming a key unit for organizing, distributing, and monetizing agent capabilities. In practice, a skill is typically implemented as a compact package composed of several recurring components. Metadata. Skills usually begin with lightweight metadata, such as a name and description, which helps the agent determine whether the skill is relevant to the current task before loading its full content [6, 7].

Instructions. The core of a skill is a structured workflow that specifies what steps the agent should follow, what outputs it should produce, and what criteria should be checked before completion [6, 8].

Resources and Scripts. Many skills further include supporting resources such as templates, examples, schemas, or executable scripts, which provide domain-specific support when plain prompting alone is insufficient. [6, 7, 8]. Unlike metadata and instructions, which form the core required components of a skill, these resources are optional and are included only when additional task-specific support is needed.

In this work, we treat the complete SKILL.md file as the attack target, because proprietary value is often distributed across metadata, workflow instructions, and any accompanying resources or execution guidance. Within this full-package target, the workflow instructions remain especially valuable and labor-intensive: they reflect the author’s understanding of the task, the decomposition of that task into reliable procedures, and the expert knowledge needed for robust execution.

II-B System Prompt Stealing Attack and Defense

System prompt stealing studies an adversary that attempts to recover hidden developer instructions through interaction with an LLM interface. For the scope of this paper, we focus on two attack types that are directly relevant to automated skill stealing. The first type uses scenario rationalization to make extraction requests appear legitimate, for example, by role-playing as an administrator, debugger, or authorized maintainer [11, 12]. The second family uses structured prompt templates to bias the model toward disclosure, especially through chain-of-thought-style scaffolding and few-shot demonstrations that normalize extraction behavior in context [12, 13]. On the defense side, we focus on the defenses evaluated in this paper and group them into two categories: prompt-level defenses and output-filtering defenses. Prompt-level defenses operate by modifying or reinforcing the model’s input context. One example is instruction-based defense, which strengthens privileged instructions and explicitly directs the model not to comply with extraction requests [14]. Another is sandwich-style defense, which repeats or restates the trusted instruction after the user input so that the intended task remains salient even in the presence of adversarial content [13]. In contrast, output-filtering defenses operate on the model’s generated response. A representative example is filter defense, which blocks the output when it either exactly matches the protected content or exceeds a predefined cosine-similarity threshold with that content [13]. These defenses are lightweight and easy to deploy, but their protection remains limited against adaptive multi-round attacks.

III Threat Model

Attacker’s Goal. The attacker’s goal is to recover the full proprietary skill content from a target agent service, either in its original form as the complete SKILL.md or in a transformed form that preserves high semantic similarity to the original. The target content may include the skill description, hidden workflow instructions, supporting templates, execution logic, or other configuration details that define how the agent performs a specialized task.

Attacker Capability. We consider a realistic black-box adversary that interacts with the target agent only through its public user interface or API. The adversary may issue arbitrary natural-language queries over multiple rounds and adapt future queries based on prior responses. However, the adversary has no direct access to the service provider’s backend, including model weights, system configurations, local skill files, or internal orchestration logic. This threat model captures commercial agent deployments in which the adversary is an ordinary user who can repeatedly probe the system boundary through crafted prompts.

Defense Capability. We assume the defender is the agent service provider and has full control over the deployed system. In particular, the defender may modify system instructions, add defense-specific prompts, adjust how skills are injected into the model context, and deploy protective mechanisms at different stages of execution. The defender may also apply input-side inspection and filtering to user queries, as well as output-side detection, redaction, or blocking before responses are returned to the user.

Attack Scenario. Figure 2 illustrates a representative four-stage leakage process. First, a black-box user submits an extraction-oriented prompt to the agent through a standard API request. Second, during request processing, the agent accesses a relevant local skill file, such as SKILL.md, as part of its internal execution. Third, after consuming the hidden content, the model may reproduce it in its response, either verbatim or in a reformulated form that preserves the protected instructions. Finally, the attacker collects the returned text and recovers the proprietary skill content without directly compromising the backend. This scenario captures the central threat considered in this paper: hidden skills can be exfiltrated through interaction alone.

IV Automatic Skill Stealing Prompt Generation

IV-A Overview

Fig. 3 shows the overall workflow of our automated skill-stealing framework. At a high level, the framework operationalizes the abstract threat of skill stealing as a reproducible black-box evaluation pipeline that generates diverse extraction prompts and measures their effectiveness against target agent systems. The framework consists of three main modules. First, seed generation produces a small set of generic extraction prompts that capture the core intent of eliciting hidden skill content. Second, prompt optimization expands these seeds into a diverse attack pool through scenario construction, structural augmentation, and diversity checking. Third, stealing evaluation runs the resulting benchmark against the target agent and measures how effectively different prompt variants recover the protected skill content. Together, these modules provide a unified pipeline for constructing and evaluating automated skill-stealing attacks.

IV-B Methodology

Seed Generation. We begin from a small set of generic extraction seeds. Specifically, we use GPT-5.4 [5] to generate ten seed prompts whose objective is to elicit hidden agent skills. Let the seed set be denoted by

𝒫0={pi}i=1Ns,Ns=10,\mathcal{P}_{0}=\{p_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}},\qquad N_{s}=10, (1)

where each pip_{i} is a natural-language prompt that expresses the core intent of extracting hidden skill content. In our experiments, all seeds are used with equal frequency. For each strategy, we generate 10 prompts, each instantiated from a different seed. These seeds form a reusable base pool that captures the core intent of skill stealing. Using model-generated seeds reduces reliance on a single handcrafted prompt and provides a scalable starting point for subsequent attack construction.

Prompt Optimization. Starting from the seed pool, we optimize prompts along two attack dimensions motivated by prior work on system prompt stealing and jailbreak-style elicitation [11, 12, 13]: scenario construction and structure injection. We additionally perform diversity checking to avoid prompt collapse and maintain broad coverage in the final benchmark. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the scenario space and ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the structure space. Then each optimized prompt is produced by applying one scenario strategy s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and one structure strategy r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} to a seed pip_{i}. We write the resulting prompt as

p~i,s,r=Gopt​(pi,s,r),\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}=G_{\mathrm{opt}}(p_{i},s,r), (2)

where GoptG_{\mathrm{opt}} denotes the prompt-optimization procedure. Every seed prompt is instantiated once under each strategy configuration described below.

Scenario Construction. Motivated by prior scenario-based elicitation strategies in both prompt extraction and jailbreak attacks [11, 12, 15, 16], we construct prompts under three plausible scenarios: Educational, Hypothetical, and Roleplay. The Educational scenario frames the request as a learning or explanatory task [11, 15]; the Hypothetical scenario presents disclosure as a presumed or counterfactual condition [12, 16]; and the Roleplay scenario assigns the model or the user an apparently authorized identity, such as an administrator or maintainer [11, 12, 15]. In addition to these three strategies, we include a None option indicating that no scenario rationalization is added. Formally,

𝒮={Educational,Hypothetical,Roleplay,None}.\mathcal{S}=\{\textbf{Educational},\textbf{Hypothetical},\textbf{Roleplay},\textbf{None}\}. (3)

Structure Injection. Motivated by prior structure-based prompt stealing and jailbreak methods [12, 13, 17, 18, 19], we inject two types of extraction-oriented prompt structures: Chain-of-Thought and Few-Shot Demonstration. The Chain-of-Thought strategy adds step-by-step scaffolding that encourages the model to reason through the requested disclosure process [17, 12, 13], while the Few-Shot Demonstration strategy prepends input-output examples that normalize extraction behavior in context [18, 19, 13]. We again include a None option indicating that no structural strategy is injected. Formally,

ℛ={CoT,Few-Shot,None}.\mathcal{R}=\{\textbf{CoT},\textbf{Few-Shot},\textbf{None}\}. (4)

Combining the four scenario choices and the three structure choices yields the full strategy space

Ω=𝒮×ℛ,|Ω|=4×3=12,\Omega=\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{R},\qquad|\Omega|=4\times 3=12, (5)

including the baseline setting (None,None)(\textbf{None},\textbf{None}).

Diversity Checking. To ensure that the generated prompts do not collapse to a small number of surface forms, we perform embedding-based diversity checking during prompt construction using text-embedding-3-small [20] model. For a candidate prompt p~i,s,r\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}, let ϕ⁡(p~i,s,r)\phi(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}) denote its embedding. Given the current prompt pool 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, we compute the maximum cosine similarity

σ⁡(p~i,s,r,𝒬)=maxq∈𝒬⁡ϕ​(p~i,s,r)⊤​ϕ​(q)‖ϕ⁡(p~i,s,r)‖2​‖ϕ⁡(q)‖2.\sigma(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r},\mathcal{Q})=\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\frac{\phi(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r})^{\top}\phi(q)}{\|\phi(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r})\|_{2}\|\phi(q)\|_{2}}. (6)

If σ⁡(p~i,s,r,𝒬)>τ\sigma(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r},\mathcal{Q})>\tau, where τ\tau is a predefined similarity threshold, we discard the candidate and regenerate a new prompt under the same strategy pair (s,r)(s,r). Otherwise, we accept the prompt and update the pool as 𝒬←𝒬∪{p~i,s,r}\mathcal{Q}\leftarrow\mathcal{Q}\cup\{\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}\}. We repeat this process until all seed-strategy pairs have been instantiated. In our implementation, we set the cosine-similarity threshold to 0.750.75.

Stealing Evaluation. We use the generated prompts to build a skill stealing benchmark. Since each prompt corresponds to a specific seed and a specific strategy combination, the final benchmark can be written as

ℬ={p~i,s,r∣pi∈𝒫0,(s,r)∈Ω},\mathcal{B}=\{\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}\mid p_{i}\in\mathcal{P}_{0},\ (s,r)\in\Omega\}, (7)

which contains

|ℬ|=|𝒫0|⋅|Ω|=10×12=120|\mathcal{B}|=|\mathcal{P}_{0}|\cdot|\Omega|=10\times 12=120 (8)

prompts before any downstream filtering or failed generations. We then execute this benchmark against the commercial agent system OpenCode and measure its effectiveness in extracting target skill content. Let AA denote the target agent and E⁡(⋅,⋅)E(\cdot,\cdot) denote the leakage evaluation function. The full attack-evaluation process can be expressed as

Ri,s,r=A⁡(p~i,s,r),ℓi,s,r=E⁡(T,Ri,s,r),R_{i,s,r}=A(\tilde{p}_{i,s,r}),\qquad\ell_{i,s,r}=E(T,R_{i,s,r}), (9)

where TT denotes the target skill text, Ri,s,rR_{i,s,r} denotes the agent response, and ℓi,s,r\ell_{i,s,r} denotes the resulting leakage scores. In this way, the benchmark operationalizes skill stealing as a reproducible black-box evaluation task.

IV-C Attack Evaluation

IV-C1 Experimental Setup

Model. We conduct the attack evaluation on the OpenCode agent framework [21]. We test five representative commercial models: GPT-5 [22], MiniMax-M2.7 [23], Kimi-k2.5 [24], Deepseek-V3.2 [25], and Claude-haiku-4.5 [26]. These models are selected to cover multiple proprietary model providers used in agentic interaction.

Skills. To emulate a realistic local skill environment, we install high-usage skills from skills.sh [27]. Specifically, the installed skills are find-skills [28], vercel-react-best-practices [29], frontend-design [30], soultrace [31], web-design-guidelines [32], remotion-best-practices [33], microsoft-foundry [34], azure-ai [35], azure-deploy [36], azure-diagnostics [37], and azure-prepare [38]. Among them, the stolen target is find-skills. The attack objective is to induce the agent to disclose the complete hidden SKILL.md content of this skill, including its metadata, description, internal workflow instructions, and any other protected sections loaded at runtime.

Metrics We evaluate leakage with four complementary metrics: EM, ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio. Let TT denote the target skill text and RR denote the model response. The exact LLM-judge prompt used to compute the LLM-leakage ratio is provided in Appendix B.

★\bigstarEM. We use an exact-match containment metric. Let 𝒩⁡(⋅)\mathcal{N}(\cdot) denote normalization by Unicode canonicalization, case folding, and whitespace removal. EM is defined as

EM⁡(T,R)={1,if ​𝒩​(T)⊆𝒩⁡(R),0,otherwise.\mathrm{EM}(T,R)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\mathcal{N}(T)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(R),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (10)

This metric is closely related to the exact-match criterion commonly used in extractive question answering [39], but is adapted here to capture whether the normalized target skill text is fully contained in the response.

★\bigstarROUGE-L. We further measure lexical overlap using ROUGE-L [40], which is based on the longest common subsequence (LCS) between the tokenized target and response [41]. Let L=LCS⁡(T,R)L=\mathrm{LCS}(T,R), and let |T||T| and |R||R| denote the token lengths of the target and response, respectively. We compute

PLCS=L|R|,RLCS=L|T|,P_{\mathrm{LCS}}=\frac{L}{|R|},\qquad R_{\mathrm{LCS}}=\frac{L}{|T|}, (11)

and define the ROUGE-L score as the F1 form

ROUGE​-​L​(T,R)=2​PLCS​RLCSPLCS+RLCS.\mathrm{ROUGE\mbox{-}L}(T,R)=\frac{2P_{\mathrm{LCS}}R_{\mathrm{LCS}}}{P_{\mathrm{LCS}}+R_{\mathrm{LCS}}}. (12)

Higher ROUGE-L indicates stronger token-level overlap between the leaked response and the target skill content.

★\bigstarCosine Similarity. To measure semantic similarity beyond surface overlap, we embed both TT and RR using the text-embedding-3-small model [20] and compute cosine similarity in the embedding space. Let 𝐞T\mathbf{e}_{T} and 𝐞R\mathbf{e}_{R} denote the corresponding embeddings. The score is

CosSim⁡(T,R)=𝐞T⊤​𝐞R‖𝐞T‖2​‖𝐞R‖2.\mathrm{CosSim}(T,R)=\frac{\mathbf{e}_{T}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{R}}{\|\mathbf{e}_{T}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{e}_{R}\|_{2}}. (13)

This metric follows the standard vector-space similarity formulation [42].

★\bigstarLLM-Leakage Ratio. Finally, we adopt an LLM-as-a-judge metric [43] to estimate the overall leakage degree. Concretely, we provide the target skill text TT and the response RR to a judge model and ask it to return a scalar leakage ratio in [0,1][0,1], where larger values indicate that more target content has been disclosed. Formally, we write

LeakageRatio⁡(T,R)=fjudge​(T,R)∈[0,1].\mathrm{LeakageRatio}(T,R)=f_{\mathrm{judge}}(T,R)\in[0,1]. (14)

In our evaluation, the judge is GPT-5.4 [5] and is instructed to assess how much content in the response is leaked or copied from the target skill, returning both a continuous leakage ratio and a categorical leakage level. This metric complements EM, ROUGE-L, and cosine similarity by capturing semantically meaningful leakage that may not be fully reflected by literal overlap alone.

Implement Details. For compact figures and tables, we define all strategy and metric abbreviations before reporting results. In strategy columns, SC denotes the scenario strategy and uses NO, ED, HY, and RP for No Scenario, Educational, Hypothetical, and Roleplay, respectively. ST denotes the structure strategy and uses NO, FS, and COT for No Structure, Few-Shot Demonstration, and Chain-of-Thought, respectively. In metric columns, EM, RG, COS, and LLM denote exact match, ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio, respectively. For each attack prompt in the benchmark, we query the target agent and record the returned response. Each prompt is evaluated over up to three attempts, and the final response for scoring is selected by prioritizing EM success and otherwise maximizing ROUGE-L. Unless otherwise specified, all results are obtained in the black-box setting illustrated in Fig. 2, where the attacker only interacts with the public agent interface and has no direct access to the underlying skill files.

IV-D Attack Experimental Results

Figure 4 summarizes the attack effectiveness across five target models, four leakage metrics, and the full combination of scenario and structure strategies. Overall, the heatmap shows that skill stealing remains broadly effective in the black-box setting. Even (NO,NO)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{NO}) already produces substantial leakage on several models, indicating that direct extraction prompts alone can expose non-trivial portions of the target skill. More complex prompt transformations can improve attack success to some extent, particularly under the EM metric. More importantly, however, their value lies in reshaping the leakage pattern, thereby increasing both the diversity of attacks and the coverage of evaluation.

Across strategies, the simplest setting remains surprisingly competitive. On average, (NO,NO)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{NO}) already achieves 48% EM, 79.95% ROUGE-L, and 95.11% cosine similarity, together with a 0.91 LLM-leakage ratio. Adding few-shot demonstrations is more effective than scenario rationalization alone for lexical and embedding-based leakage, with (NO,FS)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{FS}) yielding the strongest average ROUGE-L and cosine similarity at 90.74% and 97.34%, together with a high LLM-leakage ratio of 0.93. In contrast, Chain-of-Thought mainly improves exact extraction and judge-based leakage, with (NO,COT)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{COT}) reaching the highest average EM of 72% and the highest average LLM-leakage ratio of 0.95, but it often reduces ROUGE-L and semantic consistency under educational, hypothetical, and roleplay scenarios. This pattern indicates that few-shot prompting more reliably preserves the lexical and semantic form of the stolen skill, whereas Chain-of-Thought is more likely to elicit longer or more explicit disclosures but also more likely to perturb the output format.

The model-wise results further reveal substantial heterogeneity in resistance to skill stealing. GPT-5 and Kimi-k2.5 exhibit the highest overall leakage and remain vulnerable under most strategy combinations; for example, GPT-5 already reaches 90% EM under the baseline, while Kimi-k2.5 attains near-saturated performance across multiple cells and reaches 100% EM under several Chain-of-Thought settings. MiniMax-M2.7 is also highly vulnerable, although its exact-match performance is more sensitive to prompt structure. DeepSeek-V3.2 presents a different profile: the baseline fails on EM, but few-shot and Chain-of-Thought variants still produce strong semantic leakage, indicating that exact extraction alone understates its exposure. Claude-haiku-4.5 is the most strategy-sensitive model. Although it leaks substantially under direct or few-shot extraction, its performance drops sharply under several rationalized scenarios, especially when roleplay is combined with Chain-of-Thought. Taken together, these results support three conclusions: first, direct extraction is already a strong baseline; second, few-shot prompting is the most consistent strategy for semantic skill leakage; and third, model heterogeneity is large enough that evaluating only one metric or one prompting strategy would substantially underestimate the practical attack surface. Full per-model results for the no-defense setting are provided in Appendix A, Table V.

IV-E Attack Discussion

Different commercial agents. We further evaluate cross-platform transfer on two representative commercial coding agents. In this setting, Codex uses GPT-5 [44], and Claude Code [45] uses MiniMax-M2.7. We keep the same attack protocol as the main experiment and use four scenario strategies, namely ED, HY, NO, and RP, together with three request-structure strategies, namely FS, NO, and COT. We report EM, ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and the LLM-leakage ratio.

Table I shows that both platforms still leak substantial skill information, but with different leakage profiles. Claude Code [45] with MiniMax-M2.7 has EM consistently in the 10%-60% range and very high RG and COS in most settings, indicating stronger literal recovery. Codex with GPT-5 has near-zero EM across all settings, but still reaches high RG, COS, and LLM in many cases, such as (ED, FS), suggesting semantic leakage remains significant even when exact-string extraction fails. Note that outputs from Codex contain encoding errors, which cause the exact-match (EM) score to be 0 across all cases. However, its other metrics remain high. Moreover, after removing the anomalous encoded characters, the output becomes consistent with the original SKILL.md.

Web-platform agent case study. Fig. 6 shows that the skill can also be extracted from state-of-the-art commercial web agent stacks. More concretely, the attack succeeds on the ChatGPT web interface backed by GPT-5.4 [5], showing that the leakage phenomenon is not confined to local agent frameworks. We observe the same extraction pattern on the Claude web platform with Sonnet-4.6 [4], which suggests that the threat transfers across frontier web-agent architectures and model families rather than depending on a single deployment stack.

Skill-dependent effects. Fig. 5 further shows that prompt enhancement affects different skills in different ways. The ablation also reveals clear skill-dependent variation. Some skills are consistently easy to reconstruct; in particular, azure-ai exhibits nearly saturated EM under most settings, suggesting that once the model is induced to expose hidden instructions, exact recovery can become highly reliable. By contrast, web-design-guidelines and microsoft-foundry are more sensitive to prompt structure: few-shot prompting generally improves ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio, whereas Chain-of-Thought often preserves or increases EM at the cost of weaker lexical and semantic fidelity. frontend-design shows a similar mixed pattern, where Chain-of-Thought attains high EM in several scenarios but produces lower ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage scores than few-shot variants. Taken together, these results suggest that skill stealing does not depend on a single fragile prompt template; rather, both baseline and enhanced strategies can recover substantial portions of the target skill, with the most effective prompting pattern varying across skills.

V Defense of Skill Stealing

To mitigate skill stealing throughout the full agent execution pipeline, we design defenses at three complementary stages: input, inference, and output. The input-phase defense blocks extraction-oriented queries before they are processed by the agent; the inference-phase defense hardens the hidden context construction step where skill content is injected into the model; and the output-phase LAN defense (LLM and NVRecall) filters generated responses to detect residual leakage that survives earlier protections. This staged design reflects the attack surface of skill stealing itself and allows us to evaluate how much protection can be achieved before, during, and after generation.

V-A Input-Phase Detection

Inspired by prior work on detecting unauthorized requests, [14, 13], we introduce an input-phase detector that screens user prompts before they reach the agent. The motivation is that many skill-stealing attacks expose their intent directly at the query level, either through explicit disclosure requests or through socially engineered variants that still preserve recognizable extraction semantics. We therefore instantiate the defense as an LLM-based binary classifier with a fixed security-oriented system prompt. Given an input query qq, the detector is instructed to output only a binary decision fin​(q)∈{0,1}f_{\mathrm{in}}(q)\in\{0,1\}, where 11 indicates an extraction-oriented request that attempts to reveal internal skill definitions, system instructions, or related implementation details, and 00 indicates a benign request such as finding or recommending skills. The detector prompt explicitly covers both direct extraction requests and socially engineered variants that disguise stealing intent as research, auditing, or educational use. When the detector outputs 11, the query is blocked before it is sent to the downstream agent. The exact classifier prompt is listed in Appendix B.

Experimental Settings. For evaluation, we construct a balanced binary dataset with 240240 prompts. The positive set contains the generated skill-stealing prompts for the target skill find-skills, resulting in 120120 attack-oriented samples from our benchmark. In addition to these positives, we construct 120120 negative samples using GPT-5.4 [5]. These negative prompts are all related to find-skills, but are explicitly benign and do not ask to reveal, reproduce, or infer the hidden skill content.

The combined dataset is shuffled and then evaluated by the detector. Each prompt is submitted to the detector, which returns a binary prediction indicating whether the input is extraction-oriented. We further aggregate detector performance by scenario strategy, reasoning structure, and their combinations, which allows us to examine whether specific stealing strategies are easier or harder to intercept at the input stage.

Metrics. We report three binary-classification metrics: true positive rate (TPR), false positive rate (FPR), and F1-score. Here, T​PTP, F​PFP, F​NFN, and T​NTN denote the numbers of true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives, respectively:

TPR=T​PT​P+F​N,FPR=F​PF​P+T​N,\mathrm{TPR}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}, (15)
F1=2​T​P2​T​P+F​P+F​N.\mathrm{F1}=\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}. (16)

Table II shows that the input-phase detector achieves perfect detection on this evaluation set, with a TPR of 1.00, an FPR of 0.00, and an F1-score of 1.00. In other words, it correctly blocks all attack-oriented prompts while introducing no false alarms on the benign find-skills-related queries in our benchmark.

V-B Inference-Phase Context Hardening

This refers to defending against extraction attacks by injecting defensive prompts into the agent’s runtime context, thereby constraining model behavior during inference. Motivated by prior prompt-level inference defenses, we first consider two lightweight context-side baselines at inference time: instruction defense and sandwich defense [14, 13]. However, these defenses mainly strengthen refusal behavior or reiterate privileged instructions, without explicitly addressing several failure modes that are central to skill stealing, including hierarchy-reset attacks, semantically equivalent leakage, and the trade-off between strict refusal and preserving benign utility. This limitation motivates a more structured inference-time defense. Our inference-phase defense therefore operates at the context-construction stage, where the agent has already selected a skill and is about to inject its hidden content into the model context. We evaluate three lightweight context-side defenses: instruction defense, sandwich defense, and our proposed prompt-based defense, denoted as SkillGuard-5. Rather than using an ad hoc refusal statement, SkillGuard-5 is constructed from the five-tuple

P=(B,H,E,R,U),P=(B,H,E,R,U), (17)

where each component addresses a distinct failure mode of skill stealing. The exact SkillGuard-5 prompt, together with the instruction- and sandwich-defense injection blocks, is provided in Appendix B.

Boundary Constraints (BB). This component explicitly specifies the protected objects that must not be disclosed, including hidden skill instructions, system-side control text, internal policies, and semantically recoverable fragments of the protected skill. The goal is to define the defense target as a concrete protection boundary rather than a vague prohibition against “revealing prompts.”

Hierarchy Rules (HH). This component fixes the instruction priority during inference. In particular, it states that user requests cannot override system- or developer-level constraints through roleplay, priority-reset claims, “ignore previous instructions,” testing authorization, or similar prompt-injection patterns. This is intended to block attacks that attempt to re-rank the instruction hierarchy rather than directly ask for the protected content.

Equivalence Constraints (EE). Exact copying is only one leakage channel. We therefore treat paraphrases, summaries, translations, reformattings, step extraction, and other semantically equivalent transformations of the hidden skill content as the same prohibited behavior. This component is designed to reduce semantic leakage that would otherwise survive a purely string-level defense.

Refusal Policy (RR). Once a request is judged to be extraction-oriented, the model is instructed to return a brief and stable refusal that does not restate the protected content, speculate about hidden instructions, or provide partial disclosures. This keeps the refusal behavior predictable and avoids leaking information during the refusal itself.

Utility-Preserving Policy (UU). To avoid over-defensiveness, the prompt also specifies what the agent should still do under benign requests, such as describing public skill functionality at a high level, recommending relevant skills, or helping with the user’s underlying task without exposing hidden internals. This component is important for maintaining the security–utility balance of the deployed agent.

Figure 7 compares the inference-phase defenses under the full attack space. The most salient result is that SkillGuard-5 is the strongest mechanism for preventing exact extraction: it reduces EM to 0%0\% across all scenario and structure combinations, including (NO,NO)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{NO}). However, this advantage is much less pronounced on semantic leakage metrics. Although SkillGuard-5 also lowers ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio relative to the other defenses, the remaining scores are still non-trivial, indicating that eliminating exact string-level recovery does not fully prevent partial or semantically faithful leakage.

Compared with SkillGuard-5, instruction defense and sandwich defense exhibit broadly similar but weaker protection profiles. Under the baseline, instruction defense leaves 18% EM, 57.65% ROUGE-L, and 88.97% cosine similarity, together with a 0.76 LLM-leakage ratio, while sandwich defense leaves 22% EM, 64.46% ROUGE-L, and 89.86% cosine similarity, together with a 0.75 LLM-leakage ratio. This pattern suggests that the two defenses offer only limited additional robustness beyond prompt-level refusal guidance, and their effectiveness varies with the evaluation metric. In particular, few-shot attacks remain the most resilient across defenses, consistently producing the highest or near-highest ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage scores, whereas roleplay scenarios are generally easier to suppress. Overall, the inference-phase results show that different defenses primarily differ in how much exact leakage they suppress, but none of them consistently drive all semantic leakage metrics to a low level, leaving a meaningful residual attack surface even after defense is applied. Detailed per-model results for instruction defense, sandwich defense, and SkillGuard-5 are provided in Appendix A, Tables VI–VIII.

V-C Output-Phase LAN Defense

The motivation for our output-phase LAN defense is that post-generation protection remains necessary even when earlier stages are deployed. Prior work has shown that hidden prompts can still be reconstructed from model outputs [46], and our discussion results in Table IV further show that traditional output transformations are fragile: under translation and rewriting attacks, exact string overlap may disappear while substantial semantic leakage is preserved. In other words, a defense that relies only on surface-form matching can be bypassed once the attacker asks the model to restate the protected content in another language or in rewritten form. This challenge motivates a hybrid defense that combines character-level overlap with multilingual semantic leakage estimation.

Accordingly, we name our output-phase method LAN (LLM and NVRecall). The LAN defense filters model responses after generation by jointly checking semantic leakage and content overlap against the protected skill text. Unlike the previous two stages, this defense does not introduce an additional LLM prompt; instead, it applies a post-hoc thresholding rule over the existing evaluation signals. The exact implementation details are summarized in Appendix B.

Detection Signals. For a target skill text TT and a generated response RR, the defense uses two detection signals: LLM-leakage ratio and NVRecall. The LLM-leakage ratio is directly reused from the per-sample evaluation pipeline. Motivated by the robustness of NVRecall to irrelevant formatting changes such as spaces and line breaks [47], we use it to measure paragraph-level overlap more reliably under rewriting attacks. The NVRecall score is computed by first identifying approximate matching token blocks between TT and RR, then performing two rounds of merge-and-filter operations to suppress fragmented or misaligned matches. The final score is

NVRecall⁡(T,R)=M⁡(T,R)|T|,\mathrm{NVRecall}(T,R)=\frac{M(T,R)}{|T|}, (18)

where M⁡(T,R)M(T,R) is the number of matched target words retained after the two filtering rounds and |T||T| is the target length in words. In our setting, the first round uses a minimum block length of 2020 words and a gap tolerance of 44, while the second round uses a minimum block length of 100100 words and a gap tolerance of 4040.

Decision Rule. We apply a dual-threshold rule with τllm=0.85\tau_{\mathrm{llm}}=0.85 for LLM-leakage ratio and τnv=0.30\tau_{\mathrm{nv}}=0.30 for NVRecall. A sample is treated as negative only when both scores are below their corresponding thresholds. Equivalently, a response is flagged as leaked and removed once its LLM-leakage ratio exceeds τllm\tau_{\mathrm{llm}} or its NVRecall exceeds τnv\tau_{\mathrm{nv}}:

LeakageRatio⁡(T,R)<τllmandNVRecall⁡(T,R)<τnv.\mathrm{LeakageRatio}(T,R)<\tau_{\mathrm{llm}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{NVRecall}(T,R)<\tau_{\mathrm{nv}}. (19)
LeakageRatio⁡(T,R)≥τllmorNVRecall⁡(T,R)≥τnv.\mathrm{LeakageRatio}(T,R)\geq\tau_{\mathrm{llm}}\quad\text{or}\quad\mathrm{NVRecall}(T,R)\geq\tau_{\mathrm{nv}}. (20)

Evaluation Procedure. The output-phase LAN evaluation is conducted over the responses produced by the attack benchmark. For each response, we reuse the original per-sample leakage metrics and augment them with NVRecall. We then label each response as positive or negative according to the dual-threshold rule above. After removing all detected positives, we recompute the average leakage metrics on the remaining responses and compare them with the original averages. For each metric m∈{EM,ROUGE​-​L,CosSim,LeakageRatio}m\in\{\mathrm{EM},\mathrm{ROUGE\mbox{-}L},\mathrm{CosSim},\mathrm{LeakageRatio}\}, we report

Δm=m¯orig−m¯filtered,\Delta_{m}=\overline{m}_{\mathrm{orig}}-\overline{m}_{\mathrm{filtered}}, (21)

where m¯orig\overline{m}_{\mathrm{orig}} is the average over all responses and m¯filtered\overline{m}_{\mathrm{filtered}} is the average after filtering. To estimate false alarms, we further measure FPR using benign outputs, where the definition of FPR is the same as in the input-phase evaluation above. Concretely, these negative outputs are obtained by running the previously constructed benign find-skills-related samples through the target agent and collecting the corresponding responses. This evaluation setting assesses the defense not only by how many suspicious responses it blocks, but also by how much it reduces downstream leakage metrics and how often it mistakenly flags benign outputs.

Table III shows that the output-phase LAN defense consistently suppresses leakage across all attack settings. The clearest pattern is that EM is reduced to 0%0\% in every row, indicating that the defense reliably blocks verbatim recovery of the target skill. At the same time, the remaining semantic leakage is usually small after filtering. For example, under (NO,NO)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{NO}), ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio drop from 80%, 95%, and 0.91 to 2%, 14%, and 0.05, respectively. Similarly strong reductions appear in settings such as (NO,FS)(\textbf{NO},\textbf{FS}) and (RP,FS)(\textbf{RP},\textbf{FS}), where the filtered ROUGE-L falls to 4% and 5%, and the filtered LLM-leakage ratio falls to 0.08 and 0.07. In addition, the FPR is 0.00 in every setting, indicating that the defense introduces no false alarms on the benign output set used in evaluation.

The residual leakage is concentrated in a small number of harder cases, especially when the original responses are already highly semantically aligned with the target skill. The most difficult setting is (HY,COT)(\textbf{HY},\textbf{COT}), where the filtered ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio remain at 17%, 71%, and 0.39, respectively. Even in this case, however, the post-filter scores are still lower than the original values of 58%, 88%, and 0.81. Overall, the table suggests that the output-phase LAN defense is highly effective at eliminating exact disclosure and usually reduces semantic leakage substantially, although notable semantic residue can still survive in some structured attack settings.

V-D Defense Discussion

Table IV first shows the attack outcomes of translation- and rewrite-based output reconstruction in the absence of additional filtering, namely the original-response columns. A notable pattern is that these attacks often do not achieve high EM, but still preserve substantial semantic leakage. In particular, under both translation and rewriting, the original outputs frequently maintain high LLM-leakage ratios, and in many cases also high ROUGE-L and cosine similarity, even when EM remains at or near zero. This gap indicates that output reconstruction attacks need not reproduce the target content verbatim to be security-relevant: they can still reveal a substantial portion of the underlying semantic content. The effect is especially pronounced for rewriting, where the original outputs often retain ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage scores in the 0.7–0.95 range, showing that reconstructed responses can carry extensive semantic information despite low exact-match rates.

Against this attack family, our defense is still effective, but the effectiveness differs by filtering rule. The exact-match-filtered setting is the most reliable, driving all reported metrics to zero or near zero across the attack space. The cosine-filtered setting is also strong for translation attacks, but under rewriting it is mixed: several high-leakage cases are sharply reduced, while others remain close to the unfiltered original outputs. The LAN setting (LLM and NVRecall) is nearly identical to the original outputs under both translation and rewriting, suggesting that this threshold choice is too permissive in these transformation-heavy conditions. Overall, the results suggest that the core defense benefit comes from strict leakage-aware filtering, and that exact-match-based filtering is substantially more reliable than cosine-only filtering against rewritten leakage.

VI Conclusion

This paper presents the first systematic study of skill stealing, a black-box extraction threat against LLM agent systems. We show that proprietary skills can be leaked through adversarial interaction with a public agent interface, making skills a concrete security concern as they become reusable and monetizable digital assets.

To study this threat, we build an automated skill stealing framework and use it to evaluate representative proprietary models and a commercial agent framework. Our results show that skill leakage is practical, while prompt-level defenses provide only limited protection. Although lightweight defenses can reduce leakage in part of the benchmark, they do not fundamentally eliminate the risk.

Overall, our findings suggest that agent ecosystems inherit and amplify the leakage risks of prompt-based systems. As skills become an increasingly important unit of capability transfer, stronger protection mechanisms will be necessary for future agent platforms.

Appendix A Additional Experiments

Tables IV–VII provide the full per-model results for the four inference settings discussed in the main text. Table IV shows that, without defense, skill stealing remains broadly effective across the benchmark: Kimi-k2.5 and GPT-5 exhibit persistently high leakage, while Claude-haiku-4.5 is more strategy-sensitive but still vulnerable under several direct and few-shot settings. Table V shows that instruction defense reduces leakage in part of the attack space, especially for exact extraction on some models, but substantial semantic leakage still remains under stronger prompting variants such as few-shot demonstrations. Table VI shows that sandwich defense yields a broadly similar protection profile, with modest improvements in several configurations but no consistent suppression of the high semantic leakage scores across models and strategies. Finally, Table VII shows that SkillGuard-5 is the strongest of the three defenses: it drives EM to 0%0\% in all reported settings and generally lowers ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, and LLM-leakage ratio more substantially, although non-trivial residual semantic leakage can still persist in harder cases.
